> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Let $X,Y$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$K:X\to Y$ be a compact linear operator. The associated compact linear inverse
model has parameter space $X$, data space $Y$, forward map $K$, and admissible
truth class $X$: for a true parameter $x^\dagger\in X$, the exact datum is
$y=Kx^\dagger\in Y$. Given an exact datum $y\in Y$, solving this inverse
problem means finding a parameter $x\in X$ such that $Kx=y$. No injectivity,
surjectivity, or closed-range assumption is included in the model.

Define the Hilbert-space Moore–Penrose inverse $K^\dagger$ to have domain $$D(K^\dagger):=R(K)\oplus R(K)^\perp$$ and, for the unique decomposition $y=r+z$ with $r\in R(K)$ and $z\in R(K)^\perp$, set $$K^\dagger y:=\widetilde K^{-1}r.$$ Thus $K^\dagger y$ is the unique minimum-norm solution of $Kx=r$, and the orthogonal-range component is mapped to zero.

It is **noise-level-free** (also called **heuristic**) when the value $\alpha(z)$ for an observed datum $z\in Y$ uses only $K$, the fixed family, and $z$; it does not take the exact datum or a noise bound $\delta$ as input.

derivations.claim: For fixed $y\in D(K^\dagger)$, the output $T(y)=R_{\alpha(y)}y$ is independent of $\delta$. The exact datum $y$ belongs to every ball of radius $\delta>0$, so its error is at most $E_y(\delta)$ for every $\delta$. The assumed limit therefore forces $T(y)=K^\dagger y$.

For any $y\in D(K^\dagger)$ and $\varepsilon>0$, choose $r>0$ with $E_y(r)<\varepsilon$. Every $z\in D(K^\dagger)$ satisfying $\|z-y\|_Y\le r$ lies in that noise ball, and step 1.1 makes the reconstruction at $z$ equal $K^\dagger z$. Hence $\|K^\dagger z-K^\dagger y\|_X<\varepsilon$, proving continuity at $y$ and contradicting the hypothesis.

citations.quote:
Input a real matrix $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, data $b\in\mathbb R^m$,
and a strictly increasing finite grid $0<\lambda_1<\cdots<\lambda_q$ with
$q\ge3$. For each grid point, compute the unique Tikhonov minimizer
$$x_j=(A^TA+\lambda_j I)^{-1}A^Tb,$$
and the residual $r_j=\|Ax_j-b\|$ and solution norm $s_j=\|x_j\|$.
Discard any index with $r_j=0$ or $s_j=0$. If fewer than three indices
remain, return failure status `insufficient-valid-points`.

For consecutive retained indices $i_0<i_1<i_2$, set
$p_k=(\log r_{i_k},\log s_{i_k})\in\mathbb R^2$, $u=p_1-p_0$,
and $v=p_2-p_1$. Define their discrete curvature by
$$\kappa=\begin{cases} \dfrac{2|\det(u,v)|}{\|u\|\,\|v\|\,\|u+v\|},&\|u\|\,\|v\|\,\|u+v\|>0,\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}. \end{cases}$$
Assign this curvature to the middle retained index. Among the resulting
$q'-2$ values, return the original grid parameter whose curvature is largest;
if there is a tie, return the tied parameter with the smallest original index.
No uniform-grid spacing is assumed in log parameter. This is a finite-grid
heuristic and carries no universal optimality claim.

The output is either a selected $\lambda_j$ with its discrete curvature and
index, or the stated failure status. Every step uses a finite loop over the
input grid.

derivations.claim: For $A=I_2$ and $b=e_1$, the selector's Tikhonov formula gives $x_\lambda=(1+\lambda)^{-1}e_1$, residual $\lambda/(1+\lambda)$, and solution norm $1/(1+\lambda)$. The three grid points therefore have positive residual and solution coordinates $(1/10,9/10)$, $(1/2,1/2)$, and $(9/10,1/10)$.

The logarithmic points have increments $u=(\log 5,-\log(9/5))$ and $v=(\log(9/5),-\log 5)$. Their determinant is $-\log^2 5+\log^2(9/5)\ne0$, their norms are positive, and $u+v=(\log9,-\log9)\ne0$, so the algorithm's discrete curvature is well-defined and positive.

Exactly three indices remain, so the only consecutive triple assigns its curvature to the middle index 2. That is the only candidate for the largest curvature; the returned parameter is $\lambda_2=1$ and no tie-break is needed.

Let $V$ and $W$ be vector spaces over the same field $F$. A function

Let $X,Y$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$K:X\to Y$ be a compact linear operator. The associated compact linear inverse
model has parameter space $X$, data space $Y$, forward map $K$, and admissible
truth class $X$: for a true parameter $x^\dagger\in X$, the exact datum is
$y=Kx^\dagger\in Y$. Given an exact datum $y\in Y$, solving this inverse
problem means finding a parameter $x\in X$ such that $Kx=y$. No injectivity,
surjectivity, or closed-range assumption is included in the model.

Define the Hilbert-space Moore–Penrose inverse $K^\dagger$ to have domain $$D(K^\dagger):=R(K)\oplus R(K)^\perp$$ and, for the unique decomposition $y=r+z$ with $r\in R(K)$ and $z\in R(K)^\perp$, set $$K^\dagger y:=\widetilde K^{-1}r.$$ Thus $K^\dagger y$ is the unique minimum-norm solution of $Kx=r$, and the orthogonal-range component is mapped to zero.

For a compact operator $K:X\to Y$ between real or complex Hilbert spaces over the same scalar field, write $N(K):=\{x\in X:Kx=0\}$. For a set $M$ with $0\in M\subseteq N(K)^\perp$ and $\delta\ge0$, define $\varepsilon_K(M,\delta):=\sup\{\|x\|_X:x\in M,\ \|Kx\|_Y\le\delta\}\in[0,+\infty]$.

If $E_y(\delta)\to0$ as $\delta\downarrow0$ for every $y\in D(K^\dagger)$, then $K^\dagger$ is continuous on $D(K^\dagger).$ Thus, when $K^\dagger$ is discontinuous, no such noise-level-free rule yields worst-case convergence over each exact datum's full admissible error balls.

The power-source definition and modulus theorem with nu=1 give epsilon_K(M_rho,delta)<=sqrt(rho delta) and equality at each delta_j=rho s_j^2, witnessed by x_j=rho s_j v_j. Since these radii tend to zero, the modulus tends to zero on this restricted class; this is not the universal condition ruled out by the veto theorem.
